title: Vitamin C and Alcohol: Does It Help a Hangover? Shots, Doses, Risks
excerpt: Is vitamin C safe with alcohol, and does it help a hangover? How drinking lowers vitamin C, what the research shows, how much to take, and the truth about vitamin C shots.
metaDescription: Is vitamin C safe with alcohol, and does it help a hangover? How drinking lowers vitamin C, what research shows, how much to take, and vitamin C shots.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** vitamin C and alcohol are safe to combine at normal amounts, and topping up vitamin C is a reasonable idea if you drink, because regular drinking tends to lower your levels. But vitamin C is not a hangover cure. There is no good evidence that a vitamin C pill, an orange-juice chaser, or a trendy "vitamin C shot" prevents a hangover, sobers you up, or protects your liver from a heavy night. What it can do is cover a real gap in your diet. This guide explains how alcohol affects your vitamin C, what the research actually shows, how much is sensible, and where the vitamin C shot trend fits in.

**The quick rules:** Get 75 to 90 mg of vitamin C a day from food or a basic supplement (a little more if you smoke). If you want a supplement around a night out, 250 to 500 mg with a meal is plenty. Don't megadose: more than 2,000 mg a day mainly gives you an upset stomach and diarrhea, which is the last thing you need after drinking. Vitamin C will not lower your blood alcohol, so it never makes it safe to drive.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and official nutrition guidance. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. **Talk to your doctor before taking high-dose vitamin C if** you have a history of kidney stones, kidney disease, hemochromatosis or other iron overload, or you take medication for cancer, diabetes, or blood clotting. Get medical help right away if someone who has been drinking is confused, vomiting repeatedly, breathing slowly, or hard to wake. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning, and no vitamin will fix them. In an emergency, call 911.

## How Alcohol and Vitamin C Interact: The Mechanism in Plain Words

Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is a water-soluble vitamin your body can't make on its own, so it has to come from what you eat. It does several jobs: it helps build collagen for skin, gums, and blood vessels, it helps you absorb iron from plant foods, it supports immune cells, and it works as an **antioxidant**, meaning it neutralizes unstable molecules (free radicals) that can damage cells.

Alcohol touches vitamin C in a few ways:

1. **Alcohol creates oxidative stress.** When your liver breaks down alcohol, it first turns it into **acetaldehyde**, a toxic compound, and then into harmless acetate. Along the way, especially with heavier drinking, the process produces extra free radicals. Your body uses up antioxidants, including vitamin C and glutathione, to clean them up.
2. **Alcohol makes you lose more water-soluble nutrients.** Alcohol blocks a hormone that helps your kidneys hold onto water, which is why you pee more when you drink. Water-soluble vitamins like vitamin C and the B vitamins can be lost along with that fluid.
3. **Heavy drinking often crowds out food.** People who drink a lot tend to eat fewer fruits and vegetables, and alcohol can also reduce how well the gut absorbs some nutrients. Over time, that adds up.

The result is that people who drink heavily on a regular basis tend to have **lower vitamin C levels in their blood** than people who don't. Doctors still see occasional cases of scurvy, the classic vitamin C deficiency disease, and heavy alcohol use is one of the most commonly reported risk factors in those cases alongside very restricted diets and smoking.

For a social drinker who eats reasonably well, though, a few drinks on a Saturday won't push you into deficiency. The gap matters most when drinking is frequent and the diet is poor.

## Does Alcohol Deplete Vitamin C?

Yes, but how much depends on how much and how often you drink.

- **Occasional, moderate drinking:** unlikely to cause a meaningful drop if you eat fruit and vegetables most days. Your body holds a small reserve of vitamin C, mostly in tissues like the adrenal glands, white blood cells, and the brain.
- **Frequent or heavy drinking:** more likely to leave you low, through a mix of oxidative stress, extra losses in urine, and a worse diet.
- **Drinking plus smoking:** smoking burns through vitamin C quickly. That's why official guidance tells smokers to get an extra 35 mg a day. If you only smoke when you drink, those nights hit your vitamin C twice.

Low vitamin C doesn't usually announce itself early. Mild shortfalls can show up as tiredness and getting sick more often. More serious deficiency causes bleeding or swollen gums, easy bruising, small red spots around hair follicles, slow wound healing, and joint pain. If you notice those, see a doctor rather than self-treating. They can check your levels and look at the bigger picture. For a wider look at which nutrients drinking tends to drain, see our guide to [vitamins for hangover recovery](/never-hungover/vitamins-for-hangover).

## Does Vitamin C Help a Hangover?

This is what most people really want to know, and the answer is disappointing: **there is no good evidence that vitamin C prevents or treats a hangover in people.**

Here's what the research looks like:

- **The theory is reasonable.** Hangovers involve acetaldehyde, inflammation, dehydration, poor sleep, and oxidative stress. Vitamin C is an antioxidant, so it's natural to wonder whether extra vitamin C could soften some of that.
- **Lab and animal studies are mixed and limited.** Some older animal studies found that vitamin C helped protect against acetaldehyde's effects or nudged alcohol clearance along. Animal results often don't carry over to people, and the doses don't map neatly onto a pill you'd take after a bar.
- **Human evidence is thin.** A handful of small, older human studies looked at whether vitamin C changes how fast alcohol is cleared from the blood. Results were inconsistent and the effects, where seen, were small. None show that vitamin C reliably makes people feel better the next morning.
- **Systematic reviews haven't found a winner.** Reviews of hangover remedies, including a 2005 review in the *BMJ* and a more recent review in the journal *Addiction*, concluded that the evidence for any hangover remedy is weak or very low quality. Vitamin C is not among the remedies with a convincing track record.

There's also a practical reason vitamin C doesn't help much on the morning after: your body can only absorb so much at once. At normal intakes it absorbs most of what you take, but once you go above roughly 1 gram in a dose, absorption drops to under half, and the rest is lost in urine or stays in the gut, where it can cause cramping and loose stools.

So if you feel better after a vitamin C drink, the most likely helpers are the water, the sugar (which gives your brain quick fuel), and a bit of time. That's not nothing, but you could get the same from a glass of juice and breakfast.

## The Vitamin C Shot Trend: What's Actually in It

"Vitamin C shot" can mean two very different things, and it's worth separating them.

### Wellness shots you drink

These are the small bottles of juice, usually lemon, orange, ginger, turmeric, and sometimes cayenne, sold in grocery stores and juice bars, or made at home. Many are marketed as hangover helpers or immune boosters.

What's honest to say about them:

- **They contain real vitamin C**, often a good share of your daily need in a couple of ounces, depending on the recipe.
- **They're mostly harmless.** The ginger may help a queasy stomach a little; ginger has some evidence for nausea in other settings.
- **They're acidic.** Lemon and cayenne on an empty, already-irritated stomach can make heartburn or nausea worse for some people after drinking.
- **They're expensive for what they are.** A daily orange or a handful of strawberries gives you similar vitamin C for far less money.

We compare the popular options in our guide to the [best hangover shots](/never-hungover/best-hangover-shots).

### Vitamin C injections and IV drips

The other meaning is an injection or IV bag with vitamin C added, sold by hangover IV clinics and mobile drip services. These usually combine fluids, electrolytes, B vitamins, vitamin C, and sometimes anti-nausea medicine.

The fluids are the part that helps if you are genuinely dehydrated, and the anti-nausea medicine can help if you've been vomiting. There's no good evidence that the vitamin C in the bag adds anything meaningful for a hangover. You're paying a premium for a delivery method, not for a proven ingredient. If you're vomiting so much you can't keep fluids down, that's a reason to see a doctor or urgent care, where IV fluids are given with proper medical oversight. Our [hangover IV drip guide](/never-hungover/hangover-iv-drip) covers the costs and what the evidence supports.

## Can You Take Vitamin C With Alcohol?

Yes. There's no dangerous interaction between a normal dose of vitamin C and alcohol. You can take a vitamin C supplement on a day you drink, and orange juice in a screwdriver isn't a problem from a vitamin standpoint.

A few practical points:

- **Take it with food.** Vitamin C is acidic and can irritate the stomach, and so can alcohol. A meal helps with both.
- **Stick to a moderate dose.** 250 to 500 mg is a sensible supplement amount if you want one. Large doses just mean more of it is wasted and more chance of stomach upset.
- **Fizzy tablets add extra sodium.** Some effervescent vitamin C tablets contain a fair amount of sodium. That matters if you're watching your blood pressure.
- **Mixers aren't medicine.** Orange juice, cranberry juice, and other fruit mixers carry vitamin C, but they also add sugar and can make drinks go down faster. They don't protect you from the alcohol in the glass.

If you take prescription medicine, ask your pharmacist before adding high-dose vitamin C. Large doses can interfere with some blood glucose meters and lab tests, and they're not recommended alongside certain treatments. A normal multivitamin-level dose is rarely an issue.

## Does Vitamin C Sober You Up?

No. Vitamin C does not lower your blood alcohol content in any way you could feel or count on. Your liver clears alcohol at a fairly steady rate, roughly one standard drink an hour for many people, though this varies a lot. Nothing you swallow, whether vitamin C, coffee, water, or a greasy meal, speeds that up enough to matter.

This is important because people sometimes feel more alert after a sugary vitamin drink or a cold shower and assume they're sober. Feeling more awake is not the same as having less alcohol in your blood. **Vitamin C never makes it safe to drive.** If you've been drinking, plan another way home.

## Taking Vitamin C Before, During, or After Drinking

Because there's no good evidence that vitamin C changes a hangover, timing matters less than people think. Here's a sensible way to think about each window:

| Timing | What makes sense |
|---|---|
| Before drinking | Eat a real meal. If you take a supplement, 250 to 500 mg with that meal is fine. The meal does more for you than the vitamin does. |
| While drinking | Alternate alcoholic drinks with water. Vitamin C during drinking doesn't change how drunk you get. |
| Before bed | Water, and a light snack if you're hungry. Skip large vitamin C doses on an empty stomach. |
| The morning after | Fluids, food, and rest. Fruit such as oranges, kiwi, or berries covers your vitamin C and gives you gentle sugar. |

If you'd like a broader plan for the nights that matter, our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) walks through the habits with the best evidence: pacing, eating, hydrating, and choosing drinks wisely.

## How Much Vitamin C Do You Need?

Here are the official US figures from the National Institutes of Health's Office of Dietary Supplements:

| Group | Recommended daily amount |
|---|---|
| Adult men | 90 mg |
| Adult women | 75 mg |
| Pregnant women | 85 mg |
| Breastfeeding women | 120 mg |
| Smokers | Add 35 mg to the amount above |
| Upper limit for adults (all sources) | 2,000 mg |

A few useful comparisons:

- One medium orange has roughly 70 mg.
- Half a cup of chopped red bell pepper has close to 100 mg.
- A kiwi has around 60 mg.
- A cup of strawberries has around 85 mg.

That means most people can hit their daily need with one or two servings of fruit or vegetables. Many popular powdered vitamin C packets contain 1,000 mg, which is more than ten times the daily recommendation. That's below the upper limit, but your body won't hold onto most of it.

### Food versus supplements

Food is the better default. Fruit and vegetables come with water, fiber, potassium, and other plant compounds, and they're cheap. A supplement makes sense if you know your diet is short on produce, if you smoke, or if you drink often enough that your doctor has flagged low levels. Orange juice is a decent source too, with the caveat that it's high in sugar and acidic. Our guide to [orange juice for a hangover](/never-hungover/orange-juice-for-hangover) goes into when it helps and when it backfires.

## Side Effects and Who Should Be Careful With High Doses

Vitamin C is one of the safer supplements. Most of the problems come from megadosing.

- **Stomach upset and diarrhea.** This is the most common side effect above about 2,000 mg a day. Unabsorbed vitamin C pulls water into the gut. After a night of drinking, when your stomach is already irritated and you're already losing fluid, that's a bad trade.
- **Kidney stones.** Your body turns some vitamin C into oxalate, a building block of the most common type of kidney stone. A large Swedish study published in *JAMA Internal Medicine* in 2013 found that men who took vitamin C supplements had a higher rate of kidney stones than men who didn't. Alcohol can also leave you dehydrated, which concentrates urine. If you've had kidney stones before, talk to your doctor before taking vitamin C supplements.
- **Iron overload.** Vitamin C increases how much iron you absorb from plant foods. That's helpful for most people, but not for people with hemochromatosis (a genetic condition that causes too much iron to build up). Heavy drinking can also raise the body's iron stores. If you have hemochromatosis or have been told your iron is high, ask your doctor before supplementing.
- **Test interference.** Large doses can throw off some blood sugar meter readings and stool tests for hidden blood. Tell your doctor if you take high-dose vitamin C before medical tests.

## Vitamin C, Your Liver, and the Bigger Picture

You'll see vitamin C marketed as "liver support" and "detox." It does act as an antioxidant in the body, and researchers have studied antioxidants in people with alcohol-related liver disease. But there is no good evidence that taking vitamin C protects a healthy person's liver from heavy drinking, and it is not a treatment for liver disease. If you're worried about your liver, the steps that actually help are drinking less, getting checked by a doctor, and having blood work if you drink heavily.

It's also worth knowing where vitamin C sits next to other supplements people pair with alcohol:

- **NAC (N-acetylcysteine)** feeds the body's own glutathione production, a different antioxidant route from vitamin C. The evidence for hangovers is still limited. Our [NAC and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/nac-and-alcohol) covers what's known.
- **B vitamins** are also water-soluble and also tend to run low in heavy drinkers. See our [vitamin B12 and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/vitamin-b12-and-alcohol) for that side of the story, and our [thiamine and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/thiamine-and-alcohol) for vitamin B1, the one heavy drinkers most often run short of.
- **Magnesium and electrolytes** relate to the fluid and mineral losses from drinking. Our guides to [magnesium and alcohol](/never-hungover/magnesium-and-alcohol) and [electrolytes and alcohol](/never-hungover/electrolytes-and-alcohol) explain when they're worth it.

None of these replace the basics. A multivitamin and a decent diet cover vitamin C for most social drinkers. The supplements that get researched for the hangover itself are a different group.

## Where DHM Fits In

If you're looking up vitamin C because you want to feel better the morning after, DHM (dihydromyricetin) is the supplement our site focuses on, so here's an honest view.

DHM is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree. Researchers have studied it mainly for how it affects alcohol's action on the brain and for possible liver effects. Most of the evidence comes from animal and lab studies, plus a small amount of human data, including a 2015 randomized trial in people with fatty liver disease that found improvements in some liver markers. It's promising, not proven, and there is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers reliably in everyone.

Some DHM products also include vitamin C or other vitamins in the formula. That's fine, but the vitamin C in those blends is there to cover the basics, not because it does the heavy lifting.

If you want to try DHM, popular picks include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. Neither DHM nor vitamin C makes heavy drinking safe, and neither changes when it's safe to drive.

## The Bottom Line

- Vitamin C and alcohol are safe to combine at normal doses. There's no harmful interaction.
- Regular heavy drinking tends to lower vitamin C through oxidative stress, extra urine losses, and a worse diet. Smoking makes it worse.
- There is no good evidence that vitamin C prevents or cures a hangover, and it does not sober you up.
- Vitamin C shots and IV drips add vitamin C, but the benefit people feel most likely comes from fluids, sugar, and time.
- Aim for 75 to 90 mg a day, mostly from fruit and vegetables. If you supplement, 250 to 500 mg with food is plenty. Avoid going over 2,000 mg a day.
- Talk to your doctor first if you've had kidney stones, have iron overload, or take medication that high-dose vitamin C could affect.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is it safe to take vitamin C with alcohol?**

Yes. There's no dangerous interaction between a normal dose of vitamin C and alcohol. Take it with food, since both vitamin C and alcohol can irritate the stomach, and stick to a moderate amount such as 250 to 500 mg. If you've had kidney stones, have hemochromatosis, or take prescription medicine, check with your doctor or pharmacist before taking high doses.

**Does vitamin C help with a hangover?**

There is no good evidence that vitamin C prevents or treats a hangover in people. The idea makes sense because vitamin C is an antioxidant and drinking creates oxidative stress, but human studies are small, old, and inconsistent, and reviews of hangover remedies haven't found vitamin C to be effective. If a vitamin C drink makes you feel better, the water and sugar are the more likely reason.

**Does alcohol deplete vitamin C?**

Regular heavy drinking tends to lower vitamin C levels. Alcohol metabolism produces free radicals that use up antioxidants, alcohol makes you lose more water-soluble nutrients in urine, and heavy drinkers often eat fewer fruits and vegetables. Occasional moderate drinking in someone with a decent diet is unlikely to cause a meaningful shortfall. Smoking while drinking lowers vitamin C further.

**Does a vitamin C shot work for a hangover?**

A vitamin C wellness shot gives you real vitamin C, and ginger in some recipes may ease mild nausea, but there's no good evidence it fixes a hangover. Vitamin C added to hangover IV drips also lacks good evidence; the fluids are the part that helps if you're dehydrated. A glass of water, some fruit, and breakfast deliver much of the same benefit for far less money.

**Does vitamin C sober you up?**

No. Vitamin C does not lower blood alcohol in any meaningful way. Your liver clears alcohol at a fairly fixed rate, roughly one standard drink per hour for many people, and nothing you eat or drink speeds that up enough to matter. Feeling more alert is not the same as being sober, and vitamin C never makes it safe to drive.

**How much vitamin C should I take if I drink?**

Most adults need 75 to 90 mg a day, plus 35 mg more if they smoke, and food covers that easily. If you want a supplement on days you drink, 250 to 500 mg with a meal is plenty. The upper limit for adults is 2,000 mg a day from all sources. Going higher mainly causes stomach upset and diarrhea and raises kidney stone risk in some people.

**Should I take vitamin C before or after drinking?**

Timing doesn't matter much, because vitamin C doesn't change how drunk you get or how bad the hangover is. If you take it, take it with a meal before drinking or with breakfast the next morning. Avoid large doses on an empty stomach late at night, when your stomach is already irritated from alcohol.

**Is orange juice with vodka a good way to get vitamin C?**

It does add some vitamin C, but it doesn't protect you from the alcohol in the drink. Sweet mixers can also make drinks go down faster and add a lot of sugar. If you want the vitamin C, have the orange juice on its own with breakfast the next day.
